Made by a Catholic. This module presents Sikh scripture on its own terms. Here is how the Catholic Church speaks of it — you can explore it or leave it.

Sikhs confess one Creator, the True Name, and serve all people through seva and the langar. The Catechism (843) says the Church recognizes in other religions the search, among shadows and images, for the God who is unknown yet near, since He gives life and breath to all things.

The Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 2) teaches: “The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions.” Their ways of life and teaching often reflect a ray of the Truth that enlightens every person — yet the Church proclaims Christ, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), in whom people find the fullness of religious life.

Gurbani Jot — Amni Prayer: One God, whose Name is Truth
True in the beginning, true through the ages

column4: The Name: the presence of God, remembered and repeated in Naam simran.
The enlightener. For Sikhs the ten Gurus, and now the Guru Granth Sahib, guide the soul to God.
Selfless service, especially in the langar, the free community kitchen open to all.
Self-centeredness, the root obstacle between the soul and God.
The divine will and order that runs through all creation.
Sikhs meditate on the Name (Naam simran). Christians pray the Name of Jesus, “the name which is above all names.”
“Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God.” Christians confess one God in three Persons.

Gurbani Jot — Amni Prayer: Whatever you did for the least
column4: Seva and the langar feed all who come. Jesus said: “as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.”
Sikh scripture opens with “by the Guru’s grace.” Christians receive grace as the free gift of God in Christ.
“Every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted.”
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” “You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
